meta.title: Research studio R9: research integrity and stakeholders (the studio's own text)
meta.note: The six dilemmas are fictional, set around Prairie Town; their numbers are illustrative and no real person or organization is described. Norms are named with their primary sources and sections, checked on 3 November 2026.

norms.label: Consent
norms.sub: people agree, knowing what you will do

norms.label: Credit
norms.sub: who did what, and whose work you used

norms.label: Data licenses
norms.sub: the terms that come with data

practices.text: Tell survey participants how their answers will be used, and that they can say no.
practices.why: Informed consent: people decide with the facts in front of them.

practices.text: Get the ethics board's decision before the first interview.
practices.why: Review comes before data collection, not after.

practices.text: Write down what each author did, using a standard list of roles.
practices.why: Named [[credit-roles|contributor roles]] make authorship credit specific and checkable.

practices.text: Cite the dataset, not only the paper that describes it.
practices.why: Data are research products and deserve credit of their own.

practices.text: State who funded the study and what they saw before publication.
practices.why: Readers can weigh a funder's interest only if they know it.

practices.text: Declare that you advise the utility whose program you evaluate.
practices.why: A non-financial tie is still a conflict of interest.

practices.text: Read the data agreement before you post a co-author's data.
practices.why: The agreement, not your wish to share, sets what is allowed.

practices.text: Keep the attribution line and the license when you share an edited map layer.
practices.why: Check the layer's license: keep the attribution it requires, and follow any conditions it sets for sharing modified data.

practices.text: Say how scenarios were chosen, and report the results that weaken your story.
practices.why: Leaving out results without justification distorts the record.

practices.text: Ask the journal for a correction when you find an error.
practices.why: The published record should match what you now know.

dilemmas.title: A funder wants a headline
dilemmas.case: A regional utility association funds your study of a battery for Prairie Town. Across four scenarios, bills fall by 2 to 9% (illustrative). Its draft press release says “Batteries cut bills by 9%”.

options.text: Agree: 9% is one of your results.
options.why: It reports the best case as the result. Letting a funder shape how results are reported is an unacceptable practice in the European code (§3.1).

options.text: Ask for “2 to 9%, depending on the scenario”, and name the funder in the paper and the release.
options.why: Accurate, with its range, and the support declared (§2.7). The funder still gets a usable sentence.

options.text: Decline to comment on the release.
options.why: Your paper stays accurate, but the misleading number still goes out near your name. Better to correct it.

dilemmas.title: A convenient scenario
dilemmas.case: You ran eight scenarios. One shows a large benefit; seven show small ones. After seeing the results, a co-author suggests presenting the large one as “the central case”, with no other reason for choosing it.

options.text: Present all eight, say how each was chosen, and give the range.
options.why: Honest reporting keeps the runs that weaken the story: negative results can be as relevant as positive ones (§2.7).

options.text: Put the large one in the main text and the other seven in a supplement.
options.why: Everything is there, but the emphasis misleads: a central case needs its own justification, not its result. Say in the main text how each case was chosen.
Omitting results without justification counts as falsification in the European code (§3.1).

dilemmas.title: A co-author's data
dilemmas.case: A co-author shared hourly meter data from a rural electric cooperative (co-op) with you under a data agreement. You want to post the data with your code so that others can rerun the study.

options.text: Post it with the co-op's name removed.
options.why: A missing name does not override the agreement, and hourly meter data can still point to households.

options.text: Post it: the paper is out, so the data are public now.
options.why: Publication does not change the agreement. Posting may break it and expose the co-op's customers.

options.text: Read the agreement; post the code, a synthetic sample and how to request the data; cite the data and credit your co-author.
options.why: As open as possible, as closed as necessary: a [[synthetic-sample|synthetic sample]] lets others run the code, and the route to permission is stated (§2.5).

dilemmas.title: A community meeting
dilemmas.case: Your model ranks three sites for a solar farm near Prairie Town (illustrative). At a public meeting, residents ask why their concern about losing farmland is not in the model.

options.text: Say what the model includes and leaves out, record the concern, and report back how you treated it.
options.why: Fair process and recognition: the people affected are heard and can see what changed. Treating farmland could mean adding it as a factor, or rerunning the ranking with different assumptions.

options.text: Explain that the model is objective, so the ranking stands.
options.why: A ranking encodes choices about what counts. Calling it objective dismisses the people it affects.

options.text: Promise that the site they oppose will be dropped.
options.why: Researchers do not decide where farms go. A promise you cannot keep costs trust.

dilemmas.title: A survey without consent
dilemmas.case: A student on a project supported by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) plans to survey renters door to door next week about their energy bills, recording names and addresses. No one has asked the [[ethics-board|ethics board]].

options.text: Go ahead: a short survey is harmless.
options.why: Research with people needs an ethics determination first. For a DOE-supported study, even a survey that may be exempt needs one, from a review board, its office or their designee (§4.a).

options.text: Go ahead, but do not record names.
options.why: Collecting fewer identifiers helps, but addresses still identify people, and the survey must wait for the required ethics determination.

options.text: Pause; send the plan to the ethics board; add a consent statement; collect only what the question needs.
options.why: Prior review and informed consent, as DOE Order 443.1D requires for this DOE-supported study (§4.a); participants told how their data will be used (§2.5).

dilemmas.title: An error after publication
dilemmas.case: Months after publication you find a unit slip: one plant's capacity was entered in [[kilowatt|kW]] instead of [[megawatt|MW]] (1 MW = 1,000 kW). Fixing it changes your main result from 12% to 10% (illustrative).

options.text: Fix it quietly in the code repository.
options.why: Helpful, but the published record stays wrong. Do both.

options.text: Tell your co-authors and the journal promptly, and ask for a correction that says what changed.
options.why: Authors issue corrections promptly, and get credit for doing so (§2.7). The journal decides which kind of notice fits.

options.text: Say nothing: the conclusion still holds.
options.why: The published numbers are wrong, and others may reuse them.

items.label: You and your students
items.owed: Training, a safe place to raise a problem, and credit for the work each person did.

items.label: Co-authors
items.owed: Authorship agreed on stated criteria, contributor roles, and a say before anything is submitted.

stakeholders.ring: People the study is about or uses

items.label: Survey participants and households
items.owed: Informed consent, privacy, and only the data the question needs.

items.label: Residents near the site
items.owed: To be heard, to see how their concerns were treated, and a share in who decides.

items.label: The co-op that shared data
items.owed: The terms of the agreement kept, and the data cited.

stakeholders.ring: People who use or pay for it

items.label: The funder
items.owed: Disclosure of its support, and findings it cannot change.

items.label: The utility and the regulator
items.owed: Results with their limits, how the scenarios were chosen, and no overclaiming.

items.label: The journal and its readers
items.owed: The material results, including those that weaken the conclusion; prompt corrections; and the data or code where allowed.

items.label: Ratepayers
items.owed: A clear account of who pays and who benefits.

items.label: Future residents
items.owed: Effects that last, such as land use, counted even though they cannot speak at the meeting.

statement.label: Funding and conflicts of interest
statement.hint: Who paid, what they could see or change, and any ties of yours.
statement.planned: Who will pay, what they may see or change, and any ties of yours; “pending” if the funding is not settled.

statement.label: Contributions
statement.hint: Each author's [[credit-roles|contributor roles]]: for example conceptualization (shaping the question), data curation (cleaning and documenting data), formal analysis, writing.
statement.planned: Who will do what, in the same [[credit-roles|contributor roles]]; agree it now and check it again before you submit.

statement.label: Data and licenses
statement.hint: Each source and its terms; what is public, and the route to what is not.
statement.planned: Each source you plan to use and its terms; which ones still need permission.

statement.label: Ethics and consent
statement.hint: Who reviewed the work with people, when, and how consent was given; or “not applicable” with the reason.
statement.planned: Whether the study involves people or their data; which board or office will decide, and when; “pending” until it has.

statement.label: Stakeholders
statement.hint: Who was told, heard or consulted, and how their views were treated.
statement.planned: Who you plan to tell or consult, when, and how you will report back to them.

statement.label: Corrections
statement.hint: How a reader reports an error, and how you will correct it.
statement.planned: How a reader will report an error, and how you will correct it.

exemplars.task: Write the integrity statement for this fictional Prairie Town study, using only the facts on its fact sheet.

weak.note: Funding is not mentioned at all, and author B's advisory role on the fact sheet is a competing interest to declare.
Which data, under which terms? Public data should be cited; restricted data need a stated route.

weak.text: All participants agreed to take part
weak.note: Agreement is not informed consent, and the ethics review on the fact sheet is not named.
It hides who did what; [[credit-roles|contributor roles]] make credit checkable.

good.text: the Prairie Utilities Association funded the study; under its contract it saw the results one week before publication and could not change them
good.note: The funder is named, with its role and its limits.

good.text: author B advises the co-op on tariffs
good.note: An advisory tie is declared, not hidden.

good.text: A, conceptualization, formal analysis, writing (original draft); B, data curation, writing (review and editing)
EIA-930, public domain, cited with its access date (3 March 2026); the co-op's meter data are under an agreement that bars sharing, so the code, a synthetic sample and the request route are public
good.note: Each source with its terms: as open as possible, as closed as necessary.

good.text: the university's ethics board approved the survey before it began; each household gave written informed consent
good.note: Review before collection, and consent, both stated.

good.text: results were shown to residents and the co-op board before publication; residents asked about renters' bills, so a renter case was added and a summary sent to the meeting
good.note: One concern, the change it led to, and how people were told: they can see how their view was treated.

good.text: readers can report errors to the corresponding author; any error that changes a result goes to the journal as a correction
good.note: A route for errors, promised before anyone finds one.

diff.label: Funding
diff.good: Named, with what the funder could and could not do

diff.label: Data
diff.good: Each source with its terms and a route

diff.label: People
diff.good: Ethics review, consent, one concern and the change it led to

exemplars.note: Both statements are illustrative and use only the fact sheet; the study, the funder and the people in it are fictional.

facts.v: Would a battery at Prairie Town's co-op lower members' bills? A model on public grid data and the co-op's meter data, plus a household survey.
The Prairie Utilities Association (fictional), a regional utility association. Under its contract it saw the results one week before publication; it could not change them.
Author A shaped the question, ran the analysis and wrote the draft; author B cleaned and documented the data and edited the text.
Author B advises the co-op on tariffs.
EIA-930 hourly grid data (public domain, accessed 3 March 2026); the co-op's hourly meter data, shared under an agreement that bars passing them on.
The code and a synthetic sample of the meter data are posted with the paper; requests for the real data go to the co-op.
The university's ethics board approved it before it began; each household gave written informed consent.
Results were shown to residents and the co-op board before publication. Residents asked how renters' bills would change.
A renter case was added to the results, and a one-page summary of the change went to everyone at the meeting.

steelman.title: Should a funder see results before publication? The strongest case on each side

sides.title: For: an early look
points: A funder who knows the field can catch factual errors before they are public.
Findings that the funder has seen are more likely to be used.

sides.title: Against: no preview
points: Any preview invites pressure, even when none is meant.
Readers may suspect influence whatever actually happened.

steelman.note: A common middle path: a written agreement that the funder may comment on facts but cannot change findings, stated in the paper.

rubric.look: Your statement covers funding and conflicts, contributor roles, the terms of every data source, ethics review and consent, and how the people affected were heard.
